item.title: Valhalla's Gambit Is $8 Now: Buy, Skip, or Wait for the Next Shop
item.description:
MID GAME

The price moved from $10 to $8 and the temptation is to call that a buff. It is not. It is a discount, and the only question a discount changes is what else that money could have bought in the same shop.

**$2 is exactly one reroll.** Every shop between games offers one random piece, three random Gambits and three random tokens, with a $2 reroll. The Valhalla cut hands you back precisely one extra look.

item.title: Gambonanza Max Piece on Board: When the Upgrade Is Worth Buying
item.description:
The upgrade looks boring and it quietly decides runs. Max Piece on Board sets how many of your pieces can be on the board at once, and in a game where you lose when every piece is gone, that number is your margin.

The catch is the price. Each purchase raises the cost of the next one, so the first upgrade is cheap and the fourth is not. That curve is the whole decision: you are not asking whether more pieces are good, you are asking whether this increment is worth this price.

item.title: Gambonanza Tokens: Piece, Gambit or Tile - Which One to Take
item.description:
Three tokens sit in every shop and most players grab the cheapest one. That is usually backwards.

A Gambit token lets you pick a rarity and then choose one of three. That is the only token in the shop where you control what you get twice. A piece token gives you a random piece. A tile token gives you a random tile modifier, but you choose which square it lands on.

item.title: Gambonanza Boss Preview: What the Shop Shows You Before You Spend
item.description:
Most players shop for power. The shop in Gambonanza is not asking you to buy power, it is asking you to buy an answer, and it tells you the question first.

The preview sits in the lower-left corner of the shop, before you spend anything. It shows which boss is next and what that boss does to the board. Read it, then spend. If you skip it, you are buying blind against a rule you could have seen.
